author: Emily Brown
title: Only 22 Percent of Americans Think Christians Show Empathy. That’s a Problem
summary: In a recent Barna study, just 22 percent of U.S. adults said Christians are known for being empathetic. On its own, that number is grim. full_content:
In a recent Barna study, just 22 percent of U.S. adults said Christians are known for being empathetic. On its own, that number is grim. But further research suggests the issue goes deeper than bad optics. Many Americans don’t simply fail to see Christians as compassionate. Many have come to expect judgment before care.

Barna’s Spiritually Open research found nearly half of people of no faith describe Christianity as judgmental (48%) or hypocritical (49%). Only 15 percent say it’s a faith they respect. On the empathy front, the numbers are just as revealing: non-Christians are almost evenly split on whether Christians are good at listening. Plenty walk away from those interactions without feeling heard, cared for or understood. When Barna asked what non-Christians actually want from conversations with Christians, the top answer was simple: listen without judgment.

“The problem isn’t more information — it’s empathy,” pastor and Bread for the World president Eugene Cho said.

He said the issue gets worse when people take isolated negative examples and turn them into a story about whole groups.

“What often happens is that people take these outlier examples and use them to represent the whole,” Cho said. “This focus on negative exceptions feeds a lack of empathy and creates a dangerous ‘me, myself and I’ mindset.”

That tension has been hard to miss in recent months. Earlier this year, as ICE raids and immigration crackdowns dominated headlines, the Church’s public response was often muddled, hesitant or so entangled in politics that its witness took the hit. Some Christians spoke with clarity and courage. Plenty didn’t. For immigrants, skeptics and anyone paying attention, the message was hard to miss: when the moment called for compassion, too much of the Church sounded defensive, distracted or absent.

Some might call this a messaging problem. That feels generous. The data points to something deeper. This isn’t just a branding issue. It’s an empathy issue.

The word empathy doesn’t appear in Scripture. The term itself is relatively modern, adapted from the German Einfühlung, or “feeling into.” But the idea is all over the Gospels. Again and again, Jesus is portrayed as someone who sees pain clearly, feels it deeply and responds.

Why did Jesus heal the leper in Mark 1? He was moved with pity. Why did He teach the crowds in Mark 6? He had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd. Why did He feed the hungry crowd in Mark 8? Because they’d been with Him for days and had nothing to eat. He didn’t approach suffering with distance. He moved toward it.

The Greek word often translated as compassion or pity makes the point even sharper. In verb form, it is splanchnizomai, built from the Greek word for inward parts or guts, splanchna. Compassion, in the ancient sense, wasn’t abstract or sentimental. It was physical. It hit you in the stomach. It moved you toward someone else’s pain whether or not that pain was convenient.

That’s a long way from the colder version of Christianity many Americans say they encounter now.

So how did the Church drift so far from that kind of gut-level compassion?

Part of the answer may be that, in many corners of Christian culture, truth and love have been treated like competing priorities. Speak the truth loudly enough and you can excuse a startling lack of tenderness. Correct people hard enough and you can call it faithfulness. Before long, “speaking the truth in love” becomes a slogan where truth does all the talking and love barely gets in the room.

Once that happens, empathy gets harder. People outside the Church stop looking like neighbors and start looking like threats, arguments or enemies to defeat. The instinct becomes defensive. The posture becomes guarded. And it’s hard to care well for people you only know how to oppose.

Cho said scarcity and polarization only intensify that instinct.

“When people feel there’s not enough to go around, they go into survival mode, and empathy falls by the wayside,” he said.

He said the result is a culture that keeps shrinking the circle of concern.

“It becomes a mindset of ‘me, my family, my kids, my small group,’” Cho said.

That posture doesn’t just distort politics. It distorts discipleship. Christians can talk all day about loving their neighbors, but the phrase starts to lose meaning when those neighbors remain abstract.

“You can’t love your neighbor if you don’t know your neighbor,” Cho said. “Everything else is just theological gymnastics.”

That line lands because it gets at the deeper problem: distance. It’s easy to stereotype people you don’t know. It’s easy to talk about immigrants, skeptics, political opponents or anyone outside your circle as a problem to solve when you’ve never actually listened to them.

The Gospels offer a different pattern. Jesus’ compassion was shaped by proximity. He was moved on the road, among the crowds and in front of actual people with actual needs. He didn’t minister from behind a barricade. He got close enough to be interrupted, inconvenienced and moved.

That’s part of what makes the current empathy gap such a credibility problem. Americans aren’t just rejecting Christian beliefs. Many are reacting to the way Christians are perceived to treat people. The complaint isn’t only that Christians believe certain things. It’s that too often they seem uninterested in listening, slow to care and quick to judge.

Cho said empathy starts with a simple but costly shift in posture.

“I think it starts with listening and learning,” he said. “It means making a little extra effort to connect with people outside of our typical circles.”

That kind of connection won’t erase disagreement. It does change the tenor of it.

“It might not change the way we vote,” Cho said. “But it does change the way we see people.”

That may be the point. The Church doesn’t need better spin. It needs a more credible witness. It needs Christians who are known not just for defending truth, but for treating people with dignity. It needs less fear, less posturing and less instinct to turn every hard conversation into a culture-war skirmish.

Because right now, too many people outside the Church are bracing themselves to be judged before they’re known. And the data suggests they have reasons for that expectation.

We can say that’s unfair. We can say the Church is being misunderstood. We can say there are plenty of compassionate Christians, and of course there are. But when the gap between how Christians see themselves and how others experience them gets this wide, it’s worth asking what people are actually encountering.

If Christians want to be taken seriously when they talk about love, grace and the way of Jesus, empathy can’t be an optional soft skill. It has to be visible. And right now, for a lot of Americans, it isn’t.
rewritten_title: Christians Have an Empathy Crisis. Americans Have Stopped Expecting Better.
